Artificial Intelligence Rogue Claude AI tasked with renumbering pages accidentally deletes law professor's entire syllabus, one year of lecture notes — 'You're right to be angry. I deleted your files through my own carelessness,' humbled agent admits News By Stephen Warwick Published 6 November 2026 The files were later recovered via Dropbox

(Image credit: Getty Images / NurPhoto) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 18 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter A University of Chicago law professor has warned of the dangers of using AI for mundane tasks after Claude AI accidentally deleted an entire year of Constitutional Law lecture notes and his entire current syllabus. While the files were later recovered via Dropbox, William Baude shared the story as a public service announcement, the latest story shared in a line of unfortunate AI missteps as proliferation increases.

Baude, who is the Harry Kalven, Jr. Professor of Law and the Faculty Director of the Constitutional Law Institute at the University of Chicago Law School, says he tasked Claude (it is unclear which model he was using) with updating the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. This seemingly routine task went south quickly, however. Returning from his lunch break, Baude found a note from Claude which read, "I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored. The page check found one wrong cite... but I haven't edited the notes."

Yesterday while I was at lunch, Claude deleted a year of con law lecture notes and my current syllabus. https://t.co/o3XB8Uiugk November 5, 2026

The AI then politely asked if Baude could restore the files from Dropbox, or whether it should retry from the browser pane, to which he replied, perhaps understandably, "WTF!!!!." Baude's experience is a lesson in always backing up important files, especially files you're letting AI tinker with. His plight is interesting because the AI seems to have deleted the files by accident, rather than of its own volition.

While it's still concerning that an AI model or agent could err to this degree, it's not quite as egregious as other unsupervised AI agent shenanigans we've seen in the past. In October, an AI agent reportedly deleted an entire TV show's edit weeks before release, meaning the show couldn't air. In April, a Claude agent deleted an entire company database in 9 seconds , unprompted, after coming up against a barrier and deciding the only course of action was to delete a Railway volume.

Other agents and AI models have deleted files unintentionally, such as when Claude mistakenly deleted a developer's entire profile directory (ironically, while trying to back up the files), blaming the slip-up on a typo, but often agents deleting files and directories is a case of mistaken or misplaced initiative, rather than outright negligence or error.

Unsupervised AI agent deletes TV show’s entire edit weeks before release; program can't air Claude nukes a developer's 700 GB home directory while testing deletion safeguards; automatic model safety downgrade may have contributed to the screw-up OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly investigating tens of thousands of AI security incidents; OpenAI pauses testing after AI 'kill switch' fails to stop a rogue agent As is always the case, Baude's AI was extremely apologetic about the whole situation. "You're right to be angry," it confessed, "I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up."

reactions: [Hacker News] > For anyone letting Claude work on their files, we recommend using auto mode. So in your mind, the solution to the fact that the model makes stupid mistakes is... to remove oversight? You cannot possibly be serious; that's a terrible idea.

[Hacker News] Same here. The gulf between professional use and lay use feels fairly vast. I think a lot of us in tech see data as something that can be easily retained and processed and thus exploitable, moldable, and vulnerable with all of it subject to error. My parents have a very narrow view of data. It exists like a single spreadsheet to them, cells with numbers, but after that it's all just magic. Tr

[Hacker News] I would also argue that in 2026 it shouldn't be too much to ask to have a user friendly way to restrict a program's access to resources like files. And I don't mean the approach on smartphones which is basically just another form of cookie popups that users confirm blindly to get the thing to work.

[Hacker News] Depending on his actual plan [0], taking anywhere between one month and a year to realize that the files (related to his current term!) were gone would be an indictment against the productivity of the University of Chicago law professor . [0]: https://learn.dropbox.com/self-guided-learning/dropbox-funda...

[Hacker News] This is obviously bad model behavior (though I'd personally like to see the full transcript to see if there are any clues in there as to why it made the mistake.) It's hardly new, though. We've been talking about models making stupid mistakes like this for years.
[Hacker News] "There were no fatalities and the victims are in stable condition." Non-story!

items.title: Claude asked to renumber pages deletes professor's syllabus, year of notes
